summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a male with a history of kidney transplant, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and coronary artery disease, was admitted for severe bilateral knee pain, initially right-sided, with swelling and tenderness. He had recently been treated with antibiotics for suspected cellulitis, but symptoms persisted and spread to the left knee. Evaluation revealed a markedly elevated uric acid level of 12.3, elevated inflammatory markers, and imaging showing bilateral knee effusions, leading to a diagnosis of gout. Septic arthritis was ruled out due to lack of fever, normal white count, and negative Lyme serology. He was started on prednisone and allopurinol, with significant improvement in symptoms. Acute kidney injury, likely pre-renal from poor intake and diuretic use, resolved with IV hydration. His tacrolimus dose was increased due to a low level, and hydrochlorothiazide was discontinued to reduce gout risk. Blood pressure and diabetes management were adjusted during admission. He was discharged home on a prednisone taper, allopurinol, revised antihypertensives, and insulin regimen, with follow-up planned in rheumatology and nephrology.
problems: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic chronic kidney disease
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease with stage 1 through stage 4 chronic kidney disease, or unspecified chronic kidney disease
Atherosclerotic heart disease of native coronary artery without angina pectoris
Benign prostatic hyperplasia without lower urinary tract symptoms
